Both decisions lead to the same practical question: **how do we find the batch size that reaches the target performance in the shortest wall-clock time?**

A larger batch can be either an accelerator or a speed bump. In our experiments, a moderately larger batch with learning-rate retuning preserves learning efficiency while improving throughput. But once the batch becomes too large, the additional sample cost can outweigh the throughput gain. Figure 1 depicts this contrast as different routes to the same summit: a larger batch often helps, but it does not always get the model to the target sooner.

**What scientific principle governs this transition from acceleration to slowdown**, and **can it be turned into a measurable criterion for selecting the batch size that minimizes time-to-target**? To answer this question, we analyze batch scaling under the joint constraints of training dynamics and hardware execution, revisiting LLM RL scaling from first principles. This calls for the co-design of training algorithms and infrastructure. Our[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29296)develops the resulting framework.

# From Classical Batch Scaling to LLM Reinforcement Learning

> **How far can we usefully increase the batch?**

The modern large-batch story first became visible as an engineering breakthrough. In 2017, Goyal et al. trained ResNet-50 on ImageNet in one hour using 256 GPUs and a batch of 8,192, while preserving small-batch accuracy through linear learning-rate scaling and gradual warmup.[^goyal] The result showed that, with the right recipe, a larger batch could turn hardware parallelism into a dramatic reduction in wall-clock time. It also sharpened the next question: 

> **how far can this scaling remain effective?**

McCandlish et al. (2018) connected the point of diminishing returns to the gradient noise scale.[^mccandlish] Shallue et al. (2019) showed that useful data parallelism depends on the workload and that fair batch-size comparisons require hyperparameter tuning.[^shallue] The practical implication is simple: doubling the samples per update does not necessarily halve the updates needed to reach the same target.

A closely related question is whether changing the batch can preserve learning from a fixed number of samples. Hilton, Cobbe, and Schulman (2022) studied this as **batch-size invariance for policy optimization**: after adjusting the relevant hyperparameters, different batch sizes should produce similar learning behavior at equal sample counts.[^invariance] This is both a useful scaling intuition and a fair comparison principle: more samples should generally buy more capability, while the same cumulative sample budget should yield approximately the same capability across well-tuned batch sizes.

> **What changes in LLM RL?**

In supervised learning, examples already exist in a *fixed* dataset. Increasing the batch mainly changes gradient estimation, optimizer-update frequency, and training parallelism; the model does not have to produce its own training examples.

LLM RL adds an online loop. A Transformer agent first uses the current policy to sample responses or interact with an environment, producing trajectories and rewards. Those newly generated data are then consumed by forward passes, backward passes, and optimizer updates; the updated policy generates the next batch. **The model is therefore both the inference system that produces its training data and the learning system that consumes them.**

![LLM sampling and training share GPU computation#60%#auto#center](https://hy-model-ap-prod-1258344703.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/llm-blog/default/71e4f885/2026091516122958_72013eea4c7db8e6a838345f642a499e.png?q-sign-algorithm=sha1&q-ak=AKIDRl074nOsGdJ9zjMsCRWP3ShmgS3VtX4S&q-sign-time=1789459950;2104819950&q-key-time=1789459950;2104819950&q-header-list=&q-url-param-list=&q-signature=2fd9991431691c535c5753f36aaad19c90463bb0)

*!12 Figure 2. LLM reinforcement learning couples two GPU-intensive processes. Sampling uses autoregressive inference to produce responses and trajectories; training consumes those data to update the model. Batch size shapes both sides: generation batching determines how much inference work can run concurrently, while the training batch determines how much data each optimizer update consumes.!*

Both processes are GPU-intensive, but they exercise the hardware differently. Sampling generates one token at a time, repeatedly reads model weights, maintains KV caches, and schedules concurrent sequences. Training processes many token positions together but must store activations, compute gradients, and update optimizer states. As we show later, this computational asymmetry causes batch size to affect the two stages differently.

# Two Efficiencies, One Framework

Reaching the desired model quality sooner depends on two kinds of efficiency:

- **Sample efficiency** measures how much the model learns per training response. Batch size and its associated hyperparameters determine the progress obtained from a given sample budget.
- **System efficiency** measures how many training responses the full pipeline processes per second, accounting for generation, model updates, and waiting or synchronization.

Let $J$ denote validation performance, $N$ cumulative training responses, and $t$ elapsed time. Along a smooth approximation to a learning trajectory,

$$
\underbrace{\frac{dJ}{dt}}_{\text{Learning progress per second}}
=
\underbrace{\frac{dJ}{dN}}_{\text{Sample efficiency}}
\times
\underbrace{\frac{dN}{dt}}_{\text{System efficiency}}.
$$

If throughput doubles but learning progress per response halves, the two effects cancel. Batch size can change both factors, so we evaluate them jointly. This decomposition provides the conceptual starting point for our fixed-hardware analysis. Actual learning curves are noisy and evaluated at discrete checkpoints, so we use time-to-target for the empirical comparison.

Fix a validation target shared by all configurations. Let $N^\star$ be the number of training responses needed to reach it and $q$ the average end-to-end throughput over that interval. Then

$$
T=\frac{N^\star}{q}.
$$

Relative to a reference configuration, define the sample-cost ratio $r_N=N^\star/N_0^\star$ and throughput ratio $r_q=q/q_0$. Here, $r_N>1$ means the new configuration needs more responses to reach the target (i.e., a sample penalty), while $r_q>1$ means it processes more responses per second (i.e., a throughput gain).

### The criterion: throughput must outweigh sample cost

It is easy to see that a larger batch finishes sooner exactly when $r_q>r_N$.

::: success
Worked example
Suppose the reference configuration needs 100,000 responses at 1,000 responses per minute, so it reaches the target in 100 minutes. A larger batch needs 120,000 responses but processes 1,500 responses per minute. Then $r_N=1.2$, $r_q=1.5$, and

$$
\frac{T}{T_0}=\frac{r_N}{r_q} = \frac{1.2}{1.5}=0.8.
$$

The larger batch is 20% faster even though it is less sample-efficient, because the 50% throughput gain exceeds the 20% sample penalty. If throughput improved by only 10%, the ratio would instead be $1.2/1.1\approx1.09$, making the run about 9% slower.
:::

This relationship gives two complementary views:

- **In theory, compare throughput gain with sample penalty.** A larger batch reduces time-to-target only when $r_q>r_N$.
- **In practice, establish invariance before optimizing throughput.** Following the batch-size-invariance principle, retune batch-dependent hyperparameters and identify a range in which learning curves approximately align at equal cumulative response counts. Within that range, $r_N\approx1$, so higher end-to-end throughput translates more directly into shorter time-to-target. 

::: primary
Takeaway
Batch size affects both learning per response and end-to-end throughput. A larger batch reduces training time when its throughput gain outweighs any increase in the responses needed to reach the same quality. A simpler practical guideline is to first establish approximate batch-size invariance, then optimize throughput within that range.
:::

# Step 1: Preserve Learning per Sample

The first goal is to establish (approximate) batch-size invariance. Its implication is straightforward:
 doubling the batch should roughly halve the optimizer updates needed to reach the same model quality, leaving the total sample requirement approximately unchanged. 
 
 After separately retuning batch-dependent hyperparameters, a fair and intuitive scaling comparison should satisfy two expectations: 
- More samples should generally improve performance.
- At the same cumulative sample count, well-tuned runs with different batch sizes should achieve approximately the same performance.

Unfortunately, this does **not** happen automatically. A larger batch averages gradients over more responses, but it also gives the model fewer opportunities to update within a fixed sample budget. Preserving learning per response therefore requires retuning how far each update moves the policy.

**Retune the learning rate.** For Adam, we use the square-root rule as a starting point:

$$
\eta(B)=\eta_0\sqrt{\frac{B}{B_0}}.
$$

Here, $B_0$ and $\eta_0$ denote the reference batch size and learning rate. The rule is motivated by prior adaptive-optimizer scaling analysis.[^adam] We test it empirically while holding other optimizer hyperparameters fixed; jointly tuning more batch-dependent hyperparameters may further extend invariance.

To keep the comparison clean, we evaluate GRPO and PPO using our in-house training infrastructure. Both workloads use one global optimizer update per rollout batch, without minibatch subdivision or rollout reuse, avoiding additional tuning dimensions from minibatch size and optimization epochs.  Because training is stochastic and evaluation is noisy, we expect batch-size invariance to appear as approximate alignment, rather than exact overlap, between empirical learning curves.

### Finding I. Approximate invariance holds over a substantial, bounded range

**GRPO:** These experiments use Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 on a filtered subset of DAPO-MATH-17K, with $G=8$ responses per prompt. We evaluate mean@32 averaged over AIME 2024 and 2025. A training sample is a response retained after filtering and used in an optimizer update; each update contains $P$ retained prompt groups, giving $B_{\mathrm{train}}=PG$.

With learning-rate retuning, GRPO maintains approximately aligned sample-indexed learning curves across a 16-fold increase in prompt batch size. The left panel of Figure 3 shows this alignment from $P=64$ to $P=1024$ over the measured training window. At $P=2048$ and $P=4096$, the curves fall below this family at matched sample counts.
